neighbours.q: Why don't antibiotics work against viruses like the flu?
neighbours.label: medfacts
neighbours.reply:
Antibiotics are designed to target and kill bacteria. They work by interfering with the processes that bacteria need to survive and reproduce, such as attacking their cell walls or disrupting their ability to produce essential proteins.

Viruses, on the other hand, are much smaller and have a different structure and way of replicating. They don't have cell walls like bacteria, and they don't have the same cellular machinery that antibiotics target. Because of this fundamental difference, antibiotics are ineffective against viruses.

Think of it like trying to use a tool designed to open a lock on a door (antibiotic) to fix a broken window (virus). The tool simply isn't designed for that specific task.

So, when you have a viral infection like the flu, antibiotics won't help because they can't target the virus. Instead, antiviral medications are used to treat viral infections. These medications work by interfering with the virus's ability to replicate or infect cells.
